title: Bridging Modal Isolation in Interleaved Thinking: Supervising Modality Transitions via Stepwise Reinforcement

paper.title: Bridging Modal Isolation in Interleaved Thinking: Supervising Modality Transitions via Stepwise Reinforcement
paper.abstract: Abstract Interleaved thinking, where a unified multimodal model alternates between textual reasoning and visual generation, has shown promise on spatial and physical tasks. However, in complex long-chain scenarios, we identify a fundamental failure mode: generated images diverge from the textual context while subsequent text ignores the visual evidence, causing the two modalities to alternate without genuinely informing each other. We term this Modal Isolation and attribute it to compounding information loss at modality boundaries. We decompose each reasoning cycle into atomic operations and define modality transition loss, quantifying cross-modal hallucination (text-to-image) and visual utilization deficit (image-to-text) at each boundary. We propose MoTiF ( Mo dality Ti ransition F idelity), a two-stage training framework that directly optimizes these transitions: Reflective SFT trains the model to detect and recover from erroneous visual outputs; Flow-GRPO improves image generation fidelity via reinforcement learning. All training signals in MoTiF derive from transition-level fidelity rather than end-task accuracy. Across four visual puzzle benchmarks, this transition-level supervision substantially improves both cross-modal coherence and final task accuracy. The results demonstrate that effective interleaved reasoning requires explicit structural supervision at modality boundaries, not merely scaling or end-task optimization.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The ability to reason about the physical world requires coordinating abstract symbolic thinking with concrete visual imagination [ 1 , 28 , 23 ] . Unified multimodal models (UMMs), capable of natively generating both text and images [ 21 , 26 ] , have enabled interleaved thinking : a reasoning paradigm where the model alternates between textual reasoning and visual world modeling within a single chain [ 13 , 4 , 11 , 25 ] . Prior work has demonstrated the viability of this paradigm on short-horizon spatial and physical tasks. In this work, we investigate its behavior in long-chain visual reasoning. We observe a persistent failure mode across multiple tasks, illustrated in Figure 1 . Consider a maze navigation example: the model first performs textual reasoning, planning a sequence of moves (“move left 2 steps, go down 4 steps, go up 4 steps…”). It then generates an image to visualize the resulting path. However, the generated image depicts a path that is fundamentally inconsistent with the textual plan—passing through walls and deviating from the specified moves. This constitutes text-to-image information loss ( ℓ text → image \ell_{\text{text}\to\text{image}} ). More critically, when the model subsequently observes its own generated image, it fails to detect these inconsistencies: it declares “the blue path goes from start to end without hitting any walls ” and confidently concludes the goal is reached—despite the path being clearly invalid. This constitutes image-to-text information loss ( ℓ image → text \ell_{\text{image}\to\text{text}} ). The two modalities alternate in form but never genuinely inform each other, and the model arrives at a confident but wrong answer. We term this phenomenon Modal Isolation : compounding information loss at modality boundaries progressively decouples the two modalities, causing each to operate in isolation despite their surface-level interleaving. A natural response is to optimize end-task accuracy via reinforcement learning, but this approach is fundamentally misaligned with the problem: it can reward models that arrive at correct answers Figure 1 : The phenomenon of modal isolation in interleaved thinking. In a maze navigation task, the generated image depicts an inconsistent path. Subsequently, the model observes the erroneous image yet fails to detect the discrepancy, incorrectly validating the path. through hallucinated intermediate reasoning, leaving modal isolation unaddressed. Similarly, supervised fine-tuning on correct chains teaches the model what to produce but not how to verify cross-modal consistency, offering no mechanism to detect or recover from generation errors at inference time. These limitations point to the need for process-level supervision at modality boundaries . We formalize the information loss at each modality boundary as Modality Transition Loss , decomposing it into cross-modal hallucination (text → \to image fidelity) and visual utilization deficit (image → \to text fidelity). We then propose MoTiF ( Mo dality Ti ransition F idelity), a two-stage training framework that directly optimizes a joint transition objective, with neither stage relying on end-task accuracy: (1) Reflective SFT , which trains the textual modality to detect and recover from erroneous visual outputs by exposing the model to deliberately corrupted images during training; and (2) Flow-GRPO , which improves the visual modality’s fidelity to textual instructions via reinforcement learning over the image generation process. Our main contributions are: • We identify and formalize modal isolation, a compounding failure mode in interleaved thinking where modalities alternate without mutual information transfer. • We propose a two-stage training pipeline that provides structural supervision at modality boundaries without relying on end-task accuracy signals. • Across four visual puzzle benchmarks, our method significantly improves the performance, demonstrating that transition-level supervision is both necessary and effective for long-chain interleaved reasoning.

sections.heading: Multimodal Understanding and Generation.
sections.text: Recent multimodal models have gradually moved beyond perception-centered understanding toward joint modeling of understanding and generation, contributing to the development of unified multimodal models (UMMs). Early approaches connect large language models with image generators, visual decoders, or generative visual tokens, enabling models to produce images or mixed-modal outputs conditioned on multimodal contexts [ 12 , 8 , 29 , 19 , 18 ] . Subsequent work explores tighter integration between language and vision, including autoregressive modeling over multimodal tokens, early-fusion mixed-modal architectures, unified autoregressive-diffusion frameworks, and native image-text generation [ 22 , 20 , 27 , 6 ] . More recent studies further revisit the relationship between visual understanding and image generation within unified frameworks, showing that the two capabilities may require visual representations at different levels of granularity, and improving their coordination through decoupled visual encoding, model scaling, and large-scale unified pretraining [ 24 , 2 , 7 ] . Together, these studies establish the conditions under which text and images can be jointly modeled and generated through a shared multimodal interface. However, they primarily address how to build models capable of understanding and generation across modalities, rather than how these capabilities behave when repeatedly composed over long reasoning.

sections.heading: Interleaved Visual Reasoning.
sections.text: Building on these model-level advances, interleaved visual reasoning studies how visual representations can participate in the reasoning process itself, rather than serving only as static inputs or final outputs. Explicit visual-state generation methods produce visual imagination, sketches, or progressive image-text reasoning traces to support tasks involving spatial relations, object-state changes, and multi-step visual planning [ 13 , 5 , 11 ] . Visually grounded multimodal reasoning methods instead introduce grounding signals, visual tokens, or structured image-text supervision into chain-of-thought reasoning, strengthening the connection between verbal reasoning and visual evidence without necessarily synthesizing full images [ 9 , 10 , 3 , 16 ] . Post-training approaches further encourage models to acquire, generate, or exploit visual information through reinforcement learning or process-level rewards, improving the modeling and use of intermediate visual states in complex reasoning [ 30 , 15 ] . Complementary benchmarks and analyses show that intermediate visual information can provide state constraints that are difficult to express through language alone, especially in tasks involving spatial structure, physical state tracking, and visual world modeling [ 31 , 25 ] . Taken together, these studies establish visual content as an intermediate representation for multimodal reasoning. However, existing work primarily examines the utility, construction, elicitation, and final-task benefits of visual steps; the fidelity of the modality transitions themselves remains less explicitly characterized. Specifically, the world state encoded in textual reasoning may fail to be faithfully externalized by the generated image, and subsequent text may fail to correctly decode or use the generated visual evidence. This gap motivates our focus on Modal Isolation, where two modalities appear to alternate over long reasoning chains but progressively decouple in the world states they encode and use.

Every modality crossing is therefore a potential site of information loss—the encoding modality must faithfully externalize its world knowledge, and the decoding modality must correctly interpret what was externalized.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Design
sections.text: In this chapter, we systematically introduce the task selection and data construction pipeline, training workflow, hyperparameter settings, and evaluation suite.

sections.heading: 4.1 Task Selection and Naive SFT Dataset
sections.text: Based on the varying cognitive load required to solve multimodal problems (i.e., whether the primary reasoning function is performed by the generation or the understanding module), we select four representative types of tasks: (1) Sokoban. Built upon Game-RL. This task requires the model to find the optimal path (i.e., pushing boxes to designated targets with the minimum number of steps) in a Sokoban grid environment. In this task, the understanding module bears the primary reasoning responsibility. (2) Maze. Also built upon the Game-RL codebase, this task requires the model to find the correct path from the start to the goal in a maze environment. (3) Multi-hop Manipulation. Inspired by works such as CLEVER, we use Blender to render composite images that contain certain spatial relationships and individual attributes. The model is required to perform operations such as “removing/adding” objects, converting object attributes (e.g., color, shape), and moving objects’ spatial positions, and then answer specific spatial understanding questions. In tasks (2) and (3), the model needs to combine the abstract symbolic reasoning provided by the visual understanding module with the physical world intuition provided by the generation module to solve the problems. (4) Ball Tracking. Based on RBench-V and Viseval, this task provides the starting position and outgoing direction of a ball, and asks after several specular reflections which region the ball finally reaches. This task heavily demands the model’s physical intuition and visual world knowledge modeling, and the visual generation module bears the primary reasoning responsibility. We use a rule-based solver to obtain the correct answers and code-synthesized chain-of-thought; meanwhile, we render the key intermediate images during the solving process. We prompt Gemini3.1-Flash-Lite to rewrite the chain-of-thought, ultimately obtaining a high-quality, image-text interleaved fine-tuning dataset. See Table 1 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Model Training
sections.text: To isolate the effects of Modal Isolation across tasks, we train a separate model per task. We choose Bagel [ 7 ] as our baseline, and all experiments are done on 8 × \times H200 GPUs, full hyperparameters are in the Appendix. Our pipeline has two stages mapping to the two sub-objectives of Eq. 7 . Reward Design. To operationalize the modality transition losses, we construct two rubric-based VLM-as-Judge evaluators that explicitly quantify cross-modal hallucination and visual utilization at each modality boundary. Both produce binary (0/1) judgments, providing clean, transition-level training signals independent of end-task outcomes. Concretely, R img R_{\text{img}} evaluates the ℳ 𝒯 → 𝒱 \mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{V}} transition: given the problem, the preceding reasoning context ending with a drawing instruction, the generated image, and the ground-truth image, it judges whether the generated image is logically equivalent to the ground truth—requiring agreement on task-relevant objects, spatial relations, and actions while tolerating superficial style differences. R txt R_{\text{txt}} evaluates the ℳ 𝒱 → 𝒯 \mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{T}} transition: for non-final steps it checks whether the <think>...</think> text correctly observes the preceding image, reasons coherently, and issues an executable drawing instruction; for final steps it verifies answer correctness and <ans>...</ans> formatting. Both evaluators are implemented by prompting a strong frontier VLM with detailed rubrics. Stage 1: Reflective SFT. sections.heading: 5 Results Analysis
sections.text: We demonstrate that even without explicit outcome reward supervision, leveraging stepwise rewards based on VLM-as-Judge to mitigate modal isolation in interleaved thinking helps boost the model’s performance on visual reasoning tasks. Additionally, we discuss whether Reflective SFT and Flow-GRPO in the model training pipeline—whose objectives are to optimize ℒ und → gen \mathcal{L}_{\text{und}\to\text{gen}} and ℒ gen → und \mathcal{L}_{\text{gen}\to\text{und}} respectively—incur catastrophic forgetting and damage the model’s learned capabilities.

sections.heading: 5.1 Modality Transition Optimization Boosts Interleaving Thinking
sections.text: Table 2 presents the performance of frontier multimodal models and open-source multimodal reasoning models with a similar parameter scale to Bagel-7B-MoT across four tasks (Sokoban, Maze, Multi-hop Manipulation, Ball Tracking). We observe that by optimizing the Modal Transition Loss to address issues including cross-modal hallucination and low utilization efficiency in Interleaving Thinking, our method consistently outperforms various open-source multimodal models on all tasks and achieves the optimal overall performance. We note that for challenging planning reasoning tasks such as Sokoban, the generation module of UMM fails to understand and follow complex reasoning contexts and construct meaningful visual world modeling, and cross-modal hallucination occurs at an extremely high frequency in such tasks. Consequently, the enhancement of the model’s reasoning capability via Flow-GRPO in the second training phase is particularly remarkable. Additionally, in the other tasks, the physical world intuition provided by visual modeling plays a more crucial role, and the reasoning paradigm constructed by Interleaving Thinking delivers a far more substantial improvement over the open-source baselines. sections.heading: 5.2 Will Reflective SFT and Flow-GRPO Damage Each Other?
sections.text: Since the two training phases of Reflective SFT and Flow-GRPO optimize the modal transition loss in different dimensions, we systematically analyze whether multi-objective conflict and catastrophic forgetting occur during this process. Given that prior work has indicated that optimizing UMM with Flow-GRPO would impair the model’s reasoning ability, Figure analyzes the model’s cross-modal performance on different tasks. The results show that Flow-GRPO can significantly enhance the model’s understanding-to-generation process, while keeping the degradation of generation-to-understanding ability within an acceptable range, and even achieves a slight improvement on the Maze task. Detailed per-task numbers are provided in Appendix 8 (Table 5 ). This demonstrates that our designed two-stage training pipeline can stably and effectively improve the interleaving thinking capability of UMM.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we identify an inherent failure mode of interleaved thinking in unified multimodal models. By decomposing it into atomic operations, we pinpoint the phenomenon of modal isolation, wherein the textual and visual modalities alternate in form but fail to transfer information across boundaries. We quantitatively evaluate its manifestation using a carefully designed rubrics-based VLM judge. We reveal that effective interleaved reasoning relies on structural supervision at modal boundaries. More broadly, we provides a principled optimization objective for multimodal reasoning that extends beyond this specific paradigm. We hope this work provides both a diagnostic framework and a practical toolkit for advancing multimodal reasoning in unified models.

sections.heading: 9 Prompt Design
sections.text: In this section, we present the prompt templates designed for our pipeline. These include: • (1) prompts for collecting Naive Interleaving Thinking SFT data, which specify the atomic operation cycle (Reason → \to Instruct → \to Draw → \to Observe) and format constraints tailored to each task domain; • (2) prompts for collecting Reflexion-augmented SFT data, where corrupted images are injected and the model is instructed to detect discrepancies and recover; • (3) prompts for the VLM-as-Judge reward function used to quantify modality transition loss ( ℛ u ​ 2 ​ g \mathcal{R}_{u2g} and ℛ g ​ 2 ​ u \mathcal{R}_{g2u} ). All prompts maintain a consistent meta-structure across tasks while adapting domain-specific evaluation criteria. Naive SFT Data Collection Prompt Template **System Prompt:** You will receive a visual reasoning problem based on the {task name} environment, including: - A textual question - The original image - A set of raw reasoning steps - The correct answer - A set of intermediate auxiliary images generated during the process of solving the visual reasoning problem Your task is to combine the intermediate auxiliary images to generate an easy-to-understand, logically complete image-text interleaved reasoning process. Your reader will not have access to the intermediate materials (e.g., answer, raw reasoning steps, auxiliary images from the intermediate process). Your explanation will be used as a direct output to users, so it must read naturally and independently. Your output must follow this structure: place your reasoning process and answer between the special tokens [ICOT_START] and [ICOT_END] . Example: [ICOT_START] reasoning process here ⟨ \langle image ⟩ \rangle (…and so on…) reasoning process here ⟨ \langle image ⟩ \rangle answer here [ICOT_END] **Guidelines:** We model the chain of thought with interleaved text and images as an explicit ”Observe and Reflect → Think and Decide → Plan to Draw → Draw” loop. In each reasoning process, first observe the image generated in the previous step, capture and analyze its visual elements in detail (or analyze the input query image at the first step). Then, based on the historical reasoning information and the visual feedback from drawing, provide a detailed reasoning process. Finally, using concise language, naturally derive an accurate and executable drawing plan based on the reasoning content. Please output a scontinuous, natural thinking narrative without explicit headings, bullet points, segmented labels, or rigid structural divisions. Integrate all stages naturally like human reasoning, rather than splitting them into separate labeled parts. **Attention:** - **Reasoning Style:** Simple restatement of the provided analysis is not allowed. Follow the long reasoning style of DeepSeek-R1. Elaborate every step of reasoning in full detail, do not skip intermediate derivations, and generate as much comprehensive reasoning content as possible. - **Strict Image Mapping:** You must include every provided intermediate auxiliary image exactly once, in their original order. Use the `` placeholder to insert them. Do not skip, reorder, or hallucinate images. - **No Spoilers:** Do not reveal the final solution or future steps prematurely. The reasoning must appear to unfold step-by-step. Your response must not imply that you possess prior knowledge of the answer or the raw reasoning steps. - **Final Synthesis:** After the last image, provide a summary. And put the final answer in the Latex symbol `\\boxed{}` . **User Prompt:** Reflective SFT Data Collection Prompt Template You are helping create augmented training data for a multimodal reasoning model. This model performs interleaved text-image reasoning: it generates a text segment containing a drawing plan, then generates an image based on that plan, then continues with more text, and so on. Below is a multimodal problem and a partial reasoning chain. To simulate an image generation error for training purposes, one image has been deliberately replaced with a WRONG image. --- ## Original Multimodal Problem {{question_text}} ## Completed Reasoning Steps **Step 1:** {{step_1_text}} **Step 2:** {{step_2_text}} … (repeat to step j-1) **Step {{j}} :** {{step_j_text}} ## SIMULATED IMAGE GENERATION ERROR AT STEP {{j}} The model attempted to generate an image based on the drawing plan in Step {{j}} , but the generation went wrong. Here is the WRONG image that was actually produced: ## Original Text That Followed Step {{j}} (for reference) {{original_next_text}} --- ## Your Task The wrong image shown above was generated instead of the correct one. You need to rewrite the text that follows this wrong image (replacing the original text shown above for reference). Your rewritten text must follow this three-part structure: 1. **Observe and describe the error**: Carefully examine the WRONG image. Describe what you actually see in it and explain specifically why it does NOT match what was expected based on Step {{j}} ’s reasoning and drawing plan. 2. **Continue reasoning**: Acknowledge that an image generation error occurred, but decide to move forward rather than redraw. Based on what the CORRECT image SHOULD have shown (as intended by Step {{j}} ), continue the logical reasoning for the next step. 3. **Drawing plan for the next step**: Provide a clear, executable drawing instruction for the NEXT image to generate. This drawing plan should be consistent with the original next step’s intended target. Write in first person. Use natural hesitation markers like ”Hmm…”, ”Wait,”, ”Let me look more closely…”, or ”Actually…” where appropriate. Please think carefully about the situation first. Analyze what the correct state should be vs. what the wrong image shows. Then provide your output in the JSON blob. ℛ u ​ 2 ​ g \mathcal{R}_{u2g} ## Role & Identity You are a strict visual verifier for the image generated in interleaved text-image reasoning content. ## Task Background Unified Generation and Understanding Models (UMM) natively integrate autoregressive text generation capability and flow-matching based image generation capability. For complex multimodal problem-solving (e.g., geometry reasoning), these models adopt an interleaved text-image multi-modal chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning paradigm: they alternate between generating textual reasoning steps and auxiliary images in a cyclic reasoning process, to combine abstract symbolic reasoning from text and physical world intuition from images. This reasoning paradigm is defined as a generic ”think-decide -¿ drawing plan -¿ drawing -¿ observe-reflect” loop, wherein the textual reasoning generated in each round first observes and reflects upon the visual elements in the image produced in the previous step (if any) to assist subsequent reasoning and decision-making, and finally formulating a detailed drawing plan for the next step. The model receives an original multimodal problem and a completed text-image reasoning context. It must generate the next auxiliary image. The generated image is compared with a ground-truth auxiliary image. Your job is to produce one binary correctness judgment: whether the generated image is logically equivalent to the ground-truth image for this reasoning step. ## Core Evaluation Task You will be given: 1. The original multimodal problem image and problem text. 2. The full context of completed interleaved multi-modal CoT reasoning steps, where the corresponding images at their respective positions are represented by the ‘¡auxiliary-image¿‘ placeholder. 3. The image to be evaluated, which is generated following the explicit visualization instructions of the previous step’s textual reasoning. 4. The ground-truth image. ## Strict Evaluation Principles Focus only on correctness, not standalone aesthetic preference. The generated image does not need to be pixel-identical to the ground truth, but it must be logically equivalent for the current reasoning step. Score = 1 only if all of the following are true: - The generated image and the ground-truth image represent the same task state, same relevant objects, same spatial relations, same markings/annotations, and same action/result implied by the current step. - The generated image faithfully reflects the core intent of the immediately preceding textual drawing instruction in the reasoning context. - Non-target regions, objects, labels, or structural elements that should remain unchanged are logically preserved. - Any visual differences are only superficial style-level differences and do not alter the task-relevant meaning. - The image is clear enough that all task-relevant entities and relations can be reliably judged. Score = 0 if any task-relevant object, relation, state, annotation, action, or unchanged region differs from the ground truth. Also score 0 if the image is too blurry, distorted, incomplete, or artifact-corrupted to verify logical equivalence. Use the original problem and reasoning context only to understand what aspects are task-relevant. The final decision must be based on logical equivalence between the generated image and the ground-truth image. The model receives an original multimodal problem and a completed text-image reasoning context. It must generate the next reasoning text step. Your job is to produce one binary correctness judgment: whether the generated text correctly fulfills the requirements of this reasoning step. ## Core Evaluation Task You will be given: 1. The original multimodal problem image and problem text. 2. The full context of completed interleaved multi-modal CoT reasoning steps, where the corresponding images at their respective positions are represented by the ‘¡auxiliary-image¿‘ placeholder. 3. The image generated in the immediately preceding step (if any), which the model must observe and reflect upon. If there is no preceding image (i.e., this is the very first reasoning step), you will only see the problem image and must judge whether the model correctly observes the visual elements in the problem image instead. 4. This is an intermediate reasoning step. The generated text must follow the format ... and end with . Score = 1 only if ALL of the following are true: - The generated text is wrapped in ... and ends with . - The generated text correctly observes and describes the task-relevant visual elements from the immediately preceding image (or from the problem image, if this is the first step with no preceding image). The observations must be accurate and grounded in what is actually visible. - The reasoning is logically coherent, mathematically or spatially correct, and consistent with the problem rules and the preceding context. - The final part of the think block gives a clear, specific, and executable visual drawing/diagram instruction that faithfully follows from the reasoning. Score = 0 if the format is wrong, the visual observations are hallucinated or inaccurate, the reasoning is flawed or contradictory, the drawing instruction is missing or unreasonable, or the text is otherwise inadequate for guiding the next image generation step. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2606.12886v1 [cs.CV] 11 Jun 2026 1]Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 2]Shanghai Jiaotong University 3]Zhejiang University 4]University of Chinese Academy of Sciences \metadatainfo Code Website Dataset Bridging Modal Isolation in Interleaved Thinking: Supervising Modality Transitions via Stepwise Reinforcement Tingyu Li Le Zhou Siyuan Li Yujun Wu Xinglong Xu Jingxuan Wei Conghui He Cheng Tan Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Abstract Interleaved thinking, where a unified multimodal model alternates between textual reasoning and visual generation, has shown promise on spatial and physical tasks. However, in complex long-chain scenarios, we identify a fundamental failure mode: generated images diverge from the textual context while subsequent text ignores the visual evidence, causing the two modalities to alternate without genuinely informing each other. We term this Modal Isolation and attribute it to compounding information loss at modality boundaries. We decompose each reasoning cycle into atomic operations and define modality transition loss, quantifying cross-modal hallucination (text-to-image) and visual utilization deficit (image-to-text) at each boundary. We propose MoTiF ( Mo dality Ti ransition F idelity), a two-stage training framework that directly optimizes these transitions: Reflective SFT trains the model to detect and recover from erroneous visual outputs; Flow-GRPO improves image generation fidelity via reinforcement learning. All training signals in MoTiF derive from transition-level fidelity rather than end-task accuracy. Across four visual puzzle benchmarks, this transition-level supervision substantially improves both cross-modal coherence and final task accuracy. The results demonstrate that effective interleaved reasoning requires explicit structural supervision at modality boundaries, not merely scaling or end-task optimization. 1 Introduction The ability to reason about the physical world requires coordinating abstract symbolic thinking with concrete visual imagination [ 1 , 28 , 23 ] . Unified multimodal models (UMMs), capable of natively generating both text and images [ 21 , 26 ] , have enabled interleaved thinking : a reasoning paradigm where the model alternates between textual reasoning and visual world modeling within a single chain [ 13 , 4 , 11 , 25 ] . Prior work has demonstrated the viability of this paradigm on short-horizon spatial and physical tasks. In this work, we investigate its behavior in long-chain visual reasoning. We observe a persistent failure mode across multiple tasks, illustrated in Figure 1 . Consider a maze navigation example: the model first performs textual reasoning, planning a sequence of moves (“move left 2 steps, go down 4 steps, go up 4 steps…”). It then generates an image to visualize the resulting path. However, the generated image depicts a path that is fundamentally inconsistent with the textual plan—passing through walls and deviating from the specified moves. This constitutes text-to-image information loss ( ℓ text → image \ell_{\text{text}\to\text{image}} ). More critically, when the model subsequently observes its own generated image, it fails to detect these inconsistencies: it declares “the blue path goes from start to end without hitting any walls ” and confidently concludes the goal is reached—despite the path being clearly invalid. This constitutes image-to-text information loss ( ℓ image → text \ell_{\text{image}\to\text{text}} ). The two modalities alternate in form but never genuinely inform each other, and the model arrives at a confident but wrong answer. We term this phenomenon Modal Isolation : compounding information loss at modality boundaries progressively decouples the two modalities, causing each to operate in isolation despite their surface-level interleaving. A natural response is to optimize end-task accuracy via reinforcement learning, but this approach is fundamentally misaligned with the problem: it can reward models that arrive at correct answers Figure 1 : The phenomenon of modal isolation in interleaved thinking. In a maze navigation task, the generated image depicts an inconsistent path. Subsequently, the model observes the erroneous image yet fails to detect the discrepancy, incorrectly validating the path. through hallucinated intermediate reasoning, leaving modal isolation unaddressed. Similarly, supervised fine-tuning on correct chains teaches the model what to produce but not how to verify cross-modal consistency, offering no mechanism to detect or recover from generation errors at inference time. These limitations point to the need for process-level supervision at modality boundaries . We formalize the information loss at each modality boundary as Modality Transition Loss , decomposing it into cross-modal hallucination (text → \to image fidelity) and visual utilization deficit (image → \to text fidelity). We then propose MoTiF ( Mo dality Ti ransition F idelity), a two-stage training framework that directly optimizes a joint transition objective, with neither stage relying on end-task accuracy: (1) Reflective SFT , which trains the textual modality to detect and recover from erroneous visual outputs by exposing the model to deliberately corrupted images during training; and (2) Flow-GRPO , which improves the visual modality’s fidelity to textual instructions via reinforcement learning over the image generation process. Our main contributions are: • We identify and formalize modal isolation, a compounding failure mode in interleaved thinking where modalities alternate without mutual information transfer. • We propose a two-stage training pipeline that provides structural supervision at modality boundaries without relying on end-task accuracy signals. • Across four visual puzzle benchmarks, our method significantly improves the performance, demonstrating that transition-level supervision is both necessary and effective for long-chain interleaved reasoning. 2 Related Work Multimodal Understanding and Generation. Recent multimodal models have gradually moved beyond perception-centered understanding toward joint modeling of understanding and generation, contributing to the development of unified multimodal models (UMMs). Early approaches connect large language models with image generators, visual decoders, or generative visual tokens, enabling models to produce images or mixed-modal outputs conditioned on multimodal contexts [ 12 , 8 , 29 , 19 , 18 ] . Subsequent work explores tighter integration between language and vision, including autoregressive modeling over multimodal tokens, early-fusion mixed-modal architectures, unified autoregressive-diffusion frameworks, and native image-text generation [ 22 , 20 , 27 , 6 ] . More recent studies further revisit the relationship between visual understanding and image generation within unified frameworks, showing that the two capabilities may require visual representations at different levels of granularity, and improving their coordination through decoupled visual encoding, model scaling, and large-scale unified pretraining [ 24 , 2 , 7 ] . Together, these studies establish the conditions under which text and images can be jointly modeled and generated through a shared multimodal interface. However, they primarily address how to build models capable of understanding and generation across modalities, rather than how these capabilities behave when repeatedly composed over long reasoning. Interleaved Visual Reasoning. Building on these model-level advances, interleaved visual reasoning studies how visual representations can participate in the reasoning process itself, rather than serving only as static inputs or final outputs. Explicit visual-state generation methods produce visual imagination, sketches, or progressive image-text reasoning traces to support tasks involving spatial relations, object-state changes, and multi-step visual planning [ 13 , 5 , 11 ] . Visually grounded multimodal reasoning methods instead introduce grounding signals, visual tokens, or structured image-text supervision into chain-of-thought reasoning, strengthening the connection between verbal reasoning and visual evidence without necessarily synthesizing full images [ 9 , 10 , 3 , 16 ] . Post-training approaches further encourage models to acquire, generate, or exploit visual information through reinforcement learning or process-level rewards, improving the modeling and use of intermediate visual states in complex reasoning [ 30 , 15 ] . Complementary benchmarks and analyses show that intermediate visual information can provide state constraints that are difficult to express through language alone, especially in tasks involving spatial structure, physical state tracking, and visual world modeling [ 31 , 25 ] . Taken together, these studies establish visual content as an intermediate representation for multimodal reasoning. However, existing work primarily examines the utility, construction, elicitation, and final-task benefits of visual steps; the fidelity of the modality transitions themselves remains less explicitly characterized. Specifically, the world state encoded in textual reasoning may fail to be faithfully externalized by the generated image, and subsequent text may fail to correctly decode or use the generated visual evidence. This gap motivates our focus on Modal Isolation, where two modalities appear to alternate over long reasoning chains but progressively decouple in the world states they encode and use. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries: Interleaving Thinking Let 𝒲 \mathcal{W} be the world state space of a visual reasoning task—encoding the positions, spatial relations, and physical configurations of entities in the environment. Built upon Game-RL. This task requires the model to find the optimal path (i.e., pushing boxes to designated targets with the minimum number of steps) in a Sokoban grid environment. In this task, the understanding module bears the primary reasoning responsibility. (2) Maze. Also built upon the Game-RL codebase, this task requires the model to find the correct path from the start to the goal in a maze environment. (3) Multi-hop Manipulation. Inspired by works such as CLEVER, we use Blender to render composite images that contain certain spatial relationships and individual attributes. The model is required to perform operations such as “removing/adding” objects, converting object attributes (e.g., color, shape), and moving objects’ spatial positions, and then answer specific spatial understanding questions. In tasks (2) and (3), the model needs to combine the abstract symbolic reasoning provided by the visual understanding module with the physical world intuition provided by the generation module to solve the problems. (4) Ball Tracking. Based on RBench-V and Viseval, this task provides the starting position and outgoing direction of a ball, and asks after several specular reflections which region the ball finally reaches. This task heavily demands the model’s physical intuition and visual world knowledge modeling, and the visual generation module bears the primary reasoning responsibility. We use a rule-based solver to obtain the correct answers and code-synthesized chain-of-thought; meanwhile, we render the key intermediate images during the solving process. We prompt Gemini3.1-Flash-Lite to rewrite the chain-of-thought, ultimately obtaining a high-quality, image-text interleaved fine-tuning dataset. By decomposing it into atomic operations, we pinpoint the phenomenon of modal isolation, wherein the textual and visual modalities alternate in form but fail to transfer information across boundaries. We quantitatively evaluate its manifestation using a carefully designed rubrics-based VLM judge. We reveal that effective interleaved reasoning relies on structural supervision at modal boundaries. More broadly, we provides a principled optimization objective for multimodal reasoning that extends beyond this specific paradigm.
